---
title: "Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear"
subtitle: "Four defensive linemen, two ways to lean them, one way to spread them out and one way to smother the middle, and how to tell which you're watching"
description: "The four-man even front from the defense's side: what makes a front even, how a strength call sets it, the 4-3 Over and the 4-3 Under and the trade each one makes (where the 3-technique goes, where the uncovered guard is, who has the edge), the wide-9 front and the run lanes it pays for its pass rush, Buddy Ryan's 46 defense and the bear front that covers the center and both guards, how an even front changes when the offense goes from two backs to three receivers, and how to name the front from the broadcast angle."
glossary:
  "Even front": "A defensive front whose down linemen are set in pairs, two on each side of the ball, with nobody head-up on the center: in practice a four-man line, the 4-3 family. Most even fronts lean one tackle onto a shoulder of the center (a 1-technique) and set the other outside a guard (a 3-technique), and the direction of that lean is what Over and Under name."
  "4-3 Over": "An even front shifted toward the offense's strength (usually the tight end): the 3-technique and one end on the strong side, the 1-technique shaded to the weak side of the center, the other end on the weak side, and the Sam linebacker off the ball outside the tight end. The guard left without a lineman on him is the weak-side guard."
  "4-3 Under": "An even front shifted away from the offense's strength: the 3-technique on the weak side, the nose shaded to the strong side of the center, a 5-technique end on the strong side and the Sam linebacker on the line outside the tight end. The guard left without a lineman on him is the strong-side guard, with the Mike over him. Often described as a 4-3 with 3-4 personnel."
  "46 defense": "Buddy Ryan's eight-man front of the 1980s Chicago Bears, named for safety Doug Plank's jersey number, not for a count of players: a bear front (the center and both guards covered), both outside linebackers on the tight end's side, the strong safety in the box as a linebacker, and usually man coverage and a blitz behind it."
  "Bear front": "A front that covers the center and both guards (a 0-technique nose and a 3-technique on each guard), so no interior offensive lineman is free to double-team or climb to a linebacker. The line of the 46 defense, now used mostly near the goal line and against heavy formations."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
#| output: false
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, Rectangle, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style, routes as r
from gridiron.play import draw_marker

GREEN = "#0f7a55"         # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]  # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
OL_KEYS = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(labels="full"):
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled LT..RT ("full") or with one letter, T G C G T ("short")."""
    short = {"LT": "T", "LG": "G", "C": "C", "RG": "G", "RT": "T"}
    return [p.moved(label=(p.key if labels == "full" else short[p.key])) for p in offense("singleback")
            if p.key in OL_KEYS]


def te(side=1, key=None, label=None):
    """An in-line tight end: Y on the right, U on the left."""
    key = key or ("Y" if side > 0 else "U")
    return O(key, "TE", -0.7, side * 4.8, label or key)


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def gap_tag(fld, p, d, w, text, color=GREEN, fontsize=8.5):
    """A gap letter in a small rounded box."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight="bold", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=1.0))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=10):
    """Mark a point (a tackle, a meeting point) with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)


def ring(fld, p, key, color=GREEN, r=1.25, lw=1.8, ls="-"):
    """A ring around a player at his alignment (drawn under the marker's label)."""
    q = p.players[key]
    x, y = _P(fld, p, q.d, q.w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), r, fc="none", ec=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=7.5))


def lane(fld, p, w0, w1, d0, d1, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """Shade a rectangular lane (a run lane, a gap) from width w0 to w1 and depth d0 to d1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=0.9, ls=ls, zorder=0.8))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, lw=1.5, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'what if' or 'intent' path through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    xs, ys = np.asarray(xs, float), np.asarray(ys, float)
    if end == "arrow":   # dashed all the way to a short solid head on the last 25% of the last leg
        hx, hy = xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])
        xs = np.concatenate([xs[:-1], [hx, xs[-1]]]); ys = np.concatenate([ys[:-1], [hy, ys[-1]]])
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)


def ghost(fld, p, d, w, label, side="def"):
    """A faint, dotted outline where a player USED to be (before a shift)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    x, y = float(x), float(y)
    if side == "def":
        fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=0.75 * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc="none",
                                        ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.2)), zorder=7))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED, zorder=7)
    else:
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.75, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.2)), zorder=7))


def bracket(fld, p, d, w0, w1, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6):
    """A bar spanning the gap(s) a player owns, with end ticks."""
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=5)
    for w in (w0, w1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d - 0.35, w), _P(fld, p, d + 0.35, w)
        fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5)


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:   # yard numbers, not technique labels
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def title(ax, text, size=8.8):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=size, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


GAPS = [(-4.0, "C"), (-2.4, "B"), (-0.8, "A"), (0.8, "A"), (2.4, "B"), (4.0, "C"), (5.95, "D")]


def gap_row(f, p, owners, d_tag=-2.2, d_bar=-3.0, d_lab=-3.75, gaps=GAPS):
    """Gap letters under the line, and below them the player who owns each gap."""
    for w, g in gaps:
        gap_tag(f, p, d_tag, w, g, fontsize=7.8)
    for (w, _), lab in zip(gaps, owners):
        bracket(f, p, d_bar, w - 0.35, w + 0.35)
        say(f, p, d_lab, w, lab, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")


# --- the chapter's fronts, all authored with the tight end (the strength) on the offense's RIGHT -------
def over_front(s=1, sam=True):
    """4-3 Over to side s: weak 5, 1 shaded weak, 3 strong, strong 5; Sam stacked outside the TE,
    Mike over the strong A gap, Will over the weak (uncovered) guard."""
    out = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -s), "5"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -s), "1"),
           D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", s), "3"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", s), "5"),
           D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, s * 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.5, -s * 2.0, "W")]
    if sam:
        out.append(D("SAM", "LB", 4.2, s * 6.2, "S"))
    return out


def under_front(s=1, sam=True):
    """4-3 Under to side s: Sam on the line outside the TE (a 9), strong 5, nose shaded strong (1),
    3-technique weak, weak end in a wide 5; Mike over the strong (uncovered) guard, Will over the weak A."""
    out = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -s) - s * 1.0, "5"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -s), "3"),
           D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", s), "1"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", s), "5"),
           D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, s * 1.9, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.5, -s * 1.1, "W")]
    if sam:
        out.append(D("SAM", "LB", 1.0, T("9", s), "S"))
    return out


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for the simulated plays --------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), enter=(), ring_r=0.85):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    snap = df[df["frameId"] == int((tmap - 0.0).abs().idxmin())]
    first = snap[snap["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                 & snap["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]
    ids = set(first["_id"]) | {"football"}
    inside = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1]) & cur["y"].between(ylo, yhi)]
    ids |= set(inside["_id"]) & set(enter)
    shown = cur[cur["_id"].isin(ids) | (cur["side"] == "ball")]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r_ in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"]))
        if r_["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r_.get("label", "") or "")
        if r_["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r_ = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), ring_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    for patch in ax.patches:
        patch.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2, after=None, enter=()):
    """Numbered frame strip. `moments` is a list of (play, t, tag)."""
    cache = {}
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(moments) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.62 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(moments):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, (play, t, tag)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, moments)):
        if id(play) not in cache:
            cache[id(play)] = tracking(play)
        fld = panel(ax, play, cache[id(play)], t, lateral, window, rings, enter)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, i)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.2f} s".replace("0 s", " s")
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}" + (f"   {tag}" if tag else ""), fontsize=8.3, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.1, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(segments, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=4.6, after=None, enter=()):
    """Web version: each (play, tag, [(t, note), ...]) segment played in turn, notes as captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.45))
    frames = []
    for play, tag, notes in segments:
        df = tracking(play)
        tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
        frames += [(play, df, float(tmap[f]), tag, notes) for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique())]

    def update(k):
        play, df, t, tag, notes = frames[k]
        ax.clear()
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, enter)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, -1)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (f"  {tag}" if tag else "")
        cur = [n for tt, n in notes if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(txt + (("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""), fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK,
                     loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=range(len(frames)), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(moments, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), after=None, enter=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=notes, rings=rings, ncols=ncols, width_in=width_in,
              after=after, enter=enter)
        plt.show()
        return
    segs = []
    for play, t, tag in moments:
        if not segs or segs[-1][0] is not play:
            segs.append((play, tag, []))
    for (play, t, tag), n in zip(moments, notes):
        for s in segs:
            if s[0] is play:
                s[2].append((t, n))
    video(segs, lateral, window, rings=rings, after=after, enter=enter)
```

First-and-10. The offense breaks the huddle with its tight end on the right. Before the quarterback
reaches the line, the defensive tackle who had been standing over the right guard jogs across to the
left guard, the other tackle slides the opposite way, and a linebacker who had been off the ball walks up
and plants himself on the line just outside the tight end, hand on his knees. The middle linebacker is
pointing and shouting one word. Two plays later the tight end lines up on the left, and this time the
tackles don't trade places at all, and the linebacker outside the tight end stays five yards back. Nobody
on the broadcast mentions it. The defense has just played two different fronts, chosen by one word and
the position of one offensive player, and each was a bet about where the run would go. This chapter
teaches you to read that bet.

**You'll be able to:**

- Draw a 4-3 Over and a 4-3 Under from the offense's strength, and say which guard each leaves uncovered,
  who owns each gap, and which runs each front is built to stop.
- Explain the wide-9 front's trade, more pass rush for bigger running lanes inside the ends, and who on
  the defense has to pay for it.
- Diagram the 46 and its bear front, and explain why covering the center and both guards breaks so many
  blocking schemes, and why offenses made it disappear.
- Show how an even front changes when the offense swaps a fullback for a third wide receiver (21 to 11
  personnel), and what stays the same.
- Name the front from the broadcast angle before the snap, using two landmarks: the tight end and the
  3-technique.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)**: the
  technique numbers as job descriptions (a **1** shaded on the center, the **3** on a guard's outside
  shoulder, the **5** on a tackle's, the **9** and the **wide-9** outside the tight end), one-gap
  (attack a gap) versus two-gap (control a blocker and read), setting the edge, and the gap accounting
  that gives every gap an owner.
- From earlier parts: **[formation strength](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)**
  (the side the defense calls "strong," usually the tight end's), **covered and uncovered** linemen and the
  A-to-D gaps from [The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd), and the
  4-3 and nickel packages from [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd).
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and plays go up the page.
*Left* and *right* always mean the offense's left and right. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the offensive
linemen (T, G and C in the smallest pictures), Y and U are tight ends, Q the quarterback, R the running
back and F a fullback. Defensive linemen are labelled with their technique number; M, W and S are the
Mike, Will and Sam linebackers; SS and FS are the safeties and $ a nickel back. Green letters are gaps,
never players. Unless a picture says otherwise, the tight end, and so the offense's strength, is on the
**right**.

## What makes a front "even"

[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) counted the
front by its players: a 4-3 has four linemen and three linebackers. Coaches count it a second way, by
*where the linemen stand*, and the second count is the one that tells the offense what it is up against.

```{python}
#| label: fig-even-odd
#| fig-cap: "Even and odd, the coach's way of counting. Left, an even front: four linemen set in pairs, two on each side of the ball, and nobody head-up on the center (green ring), so the center is free to help a teammate or climb to a linebacker. Right, an odd front: a nose head-up on the center, splitting the line into a middle man and a pair on either side. Fronts are named after this picture as much as after the head count."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9))
dfns = [("Even: 5, 3, 3, 5 (four down)",
         [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "5"), D("LT3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"),
          D("RT3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", 1), "5")]),
        ("Odd: 4, 0, 4 (three down)",
         [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("4", -1), "4"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, 0.0, "0"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("4", 1), "4")])]
for ax, (ttl, dl) in zip(axes, dfns):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dl, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.6, 7.6), window=(-3.4, 4.2), title=False)
    ring(f, p, "C", color=GREEN if "Even" in ttl else style.DEFENSE_DARK, r=1.15)
    say(f, p, 3.0, 0.0, "center free" if "Even" in ttl else "center covered",
        color=GREEN if "Even" in ttl else style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
    title(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

An [**even front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-even-front) sets its down linemen in pairs, two on
each side of the ball, with nobody head-up on the center. In practice that means a four-man line, the
family of fronts that grew up around the 4-3. An odd front puts a man on the center (the nose of a 3-4,
or the middle man of a five-man line) and is the subject of
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd).

Why does the center matter so much? Because of what you learned about *covered* and *uncovered*
linemen in [03-01](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd). An offensive lineman with nobody
on him is the offense's spare part: he can double-team a neighbor or climb to a linebacker. In an odd
front the center is busy from the first instant, and the spare parts are the guards. In an even front
the center starts free, and so does at least one guard, which is where the offense will look first.
Every even front is a decision about *which* linemen to leave free, and where to put the linebackers who
have to deal with them.

The perfectly balanced version in @fig-even-odd (a 3-technique on each guard, an end on each tackle)
exists, and you will see it on passing downs, when it gives each of the two best interior rushers a guard
to himself. On early downs, most even fronts are *unbalanced* on purpose. One tackle slides in to a
**1-technique**, shaded on a shoulder of the center, and the other stays a **3-technique**, outside a
guard. Now the line leans: the 3-technique's side has its linemen spread wide, the 1-technique's side has
them pinched in toward the ball. Which way the line leans, toward the offense's strength or away from it,
is the difference between the two fronts this chapter is built around.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Even and odd just mean four linemen or three." That's the fan's shortcut and it usually works. But the
coaches' test is the center and the pairs, and the two counts can disagree: the bear front later in this
chapter has four men with their hands down *and* a nose head-up on the center, and a 3-4 team can put a
fourth player's hand on the ground without changing who covers whom. When the counts argue, believe
the alignment.
:::

## Setting the front: the strength call

A front leans toward or away from something, so before it can line up, the defense needs a word for
which side is which. That word is the **strength**, the side the defense calls strong, from
[Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).
For fronts, the usual rule is simple: **the strength is the tight end's side.** The tight end is a sixth
blocker attached to the line, so his side has one more gap (the D gap outside him) and one more man to
block with. Runs go there more often, and the front wants to know about it.

When there is no tight end, or one on each side, defenses fall back on other rules. Common ones are the
*field* (the wide side of the field when the ball is on a hash), the *running back* (the side he is
offset to in the shotgun), or the side with more receivers. Which rule a team uses, and in what order,
is in its playbook, and the call before the snap says which one applies.

The call is relative, and that is the whole point. The defense does not call "3-technique on the left
guard." It calls something like "Over" and lets the formation decide which guard: **Over** means the line
leans *toward* the strength, **Under** means it leans *away* from it.[^broaddus] A Mike linebacker
shouting "Strong right! Over!" is translating one word into eleven alignments for this particular snap.

## The 4-3 Over

```{python}
#| label: fig-over-under
#| fig-cap: "The two even fronts against the same offense (tight end on the right; the backs of the I-formation are not shown). Under each front: the seven gaps (green) and the player who owns each one. Left, the 4-3 Over: the line leans toward the tight end, with the 3-technique on the right guard and the 1-technique shaded to the left of the center. The left guard has nobody on him (green ring): he is the uncovered guard, and the Will stands over him. The Sam is off the ball outside the tight end. Right, the 4-3 Under: the line leans away from the tight end, with the 3-technique on the left guard and the nose shaded to the right of the center. Now the right guard is uncovered and the Mike stands over him, and the Sam is on the line, outside the tight end. Same eleven players, same personnel, opposite bets."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
for ax, (ttl, dfn, free, owners) in zip(axes, [
        ("4-3 Over: lean toward the TE", over_front(+1), "LG", ["5", "W", "1", "M", "3", "5", "S"]),
        ("4-3 Under: lean away from it", under_front(+1), "RG", ["5", "3", "W", "1", "M", "5", "S"])]):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.6, 8.4), window=(-5.0, 6.6), title=False)
    gap_row(f, p, owners)
    ring(f, p, free, color=GREEN, r=1.05)
    title(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

Start with the left half of @fig-over-under, the [**4-3 Over**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-3-over).
On the strong side (the tight end's), the defense puts its two most active linemen: the **3-technique** on
the strong guard's outside shoulder and the strong end on the tackle, here in a 5 (some teams play him
tighter, in a 6 or 7 on the tight end, to stop the tight end blocking down). On the weak side it puts the
**1-technique**, shaded on the center's weak shoulder, and the weak end in a 5. The linebackers fill in
around them. The Mike stacks behind the line over the strong A gap; the Will stands over the weak guard;
the Sam is off the ball, a few yards outside the tight end.

Now count the gaps, the way [05-01](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) taught. Seven gaps, seven
men, one each: the four linemen take the gaps they are shaded into (weak C, weak A, strong B, strong C),
and the three linebackers take the three left over (weak B, strong A, and the D gap outside the tight end).
This is one-gap football. Every man knows his gap before the snap and can play it at full speed.

**Why lean toward the tight end?** Because that's where the offense has the most to work with. The strong
side has three blockers on the line (guard, tackle, tight end) and four gaps, and the classic power runs,
the off-tackle plays of [Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), go there.
The Over meets them with linemen. Its strong-side B and C gaps belong to big men with their hands in the
ground, not to linebackers who have to read and then come downhill, so the runs the offense likes best
run into the defense's weight. And the Sam, off the ball, is free to do two jobs: fill the D gap on a run,
or turn and cover the tight end on a pass. Play-action to the tight end is one of the oldest plays in
football; an off-ball Sam can see it.

**What does it give up?** Look at the green ring. The **weak guard is uncovered**, and an uncovered guard
on the side away from the tight end is a lineman with a clean path to the Will linebacker. That empty
patch of the line, with no defensive lineman over a blocker, is what coaches call a **bubble**, and offenses
aim runs at bubbles: the guard can help double the 1-technique and then climb to the Will, or go
straight to him. Over teams live with it by asking a lot of the Will, the run-and-hit linebacker who has
to beat a 300-pound guard to his gap. There is a second, subtler cost: the 3-technique is on the side with
the most offensive blockers, so it's the side where he is easiest to double-team.

## The 4-3 Under

Flip the lean and you get the right half of @fig-over-under, the
[**4-3 Under**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-3-under). The 3-technique moves to the *weak* guard. The
nose slides to a 1-technique on the center's *strong* shoulder. The strong end stays in a 5 on the
tackle, and the weak end, with no tight end to worry about, widens into a loose 5 or further. Then the
linebackers shift the other way: **the Sam walks up onto the line**, outside the tight end, and the Mike
moves over the strong guard.

Count the gaps again. On the strong side, the Sam owns the D gap and the end the C. The Mike, stacked over
the uncovered strong guard, owns the B gap, and the nose owns the strong A. On the weak side, the Will
owns the A, the 3-technique the B and the weak end the C. Seven for seven, just distributed differently.

**Why lean away?** Three reasons, and each one is a bet.

1. **A hard strong-side edge.** With the Sam on the line and a big end in the 5, the tight end's side has
   two defenders on the line of scrimmage outside the tackle. The off-tackle run has to block both, and
   the edge they set turns everything back inside. Seattle's defensive coordinator in 2011, Gus Bradley,
   put the whole philosophy in two sentences: "We want to set the edge. Turn everything back inside to our
   big guys."[^seattlebig]
2. **A one-on-one 3-technique.** On the weak side there is no tight end, so the offense has fewer ways to
   double-team the 3-technique without leaving someone else free. The Under puts its best interior pass
   rusher where he is likeliest to get a guard alone. Monte Kiffin's Tampa Bay defense had a name for him,
   the **under tackle**, after the side he played, and built its pass rush around Warren Sapp in that spot.
3. **A clean Mike.** The strong guard is uncovered, but the Mike is right over him, and the nose and end
   on either side of the guard make it hard for him to get a clean path up to the Mike. A guard who has to
   help the nose with a double team before he climbs arrives late.

Put the Sam on the line, lean the line away from him, and the Under starts to look like something else.
Squint at the right half of @fig-over-under: five men on the line, a nose on the center's shoulder, two big
ends, a stand-up player on the edge, two inside linebackers. That is close to a 3-4 with one outside
linebacker's hand on the ground, which is why Pete Carroll described his Seattle defense as "a 4-3 with 3-4
personnel."[^carroll] The labels in this part of football blur at the edges; the alignment is what's real.

**What does it give up?** The bubble is now on the *strong* side, over the right guard, in front of the
Mike. Runs at that bubble, inside zone and duo toward the tight end, put the uncovered guard on a
linebacker with a running start. And the Sam on the line is a Sam who can't easily drop into coverage:
if he rushes or sets the edge, someone else has to take the tight end on play-action, usually a safety.

```{python}
#| label: fig-attack-bubble
#| fig-cap: "Where each front is soft: the uncovered guard. Left, inside zone to the weak side (the offense's left) against the Over. The left guard (green ring) has nobody on him, so he helps the center move the 1-technique and then climbs to the Will (dashed green), and the back aims for the weak B gap. Right, inside zone toward the tight end against the Under: now it is the right guard who is free, and he climbs to the Mike, who has to beat a lineman with a running start to the strong B gap. Blocks are simplified (blue bars); the point is which guard is free and where he goes."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
# Over: inside zone left, at the bubble over the LG
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "C", (0.2, -0.75)); go_to(p, "LG", (0.25, -0.95))
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.0)); go_to(p, "RG", (0.3, 2.3)); go_to(p, "RT", (0.3, 3.9)); go_to(p, "Y", (2.9, 6.0))
go_to(p, "RB", (-0.9, -2.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, -0.7)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.2, 0.6), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-8.2, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 7.0), title=False)
ring(f, p, "LG", color=GREEN, r=1.05)
dashed(f, p, [(0.6, -1.4), (2.4, -1.9), (3.65, -2.0)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
say(f, p, 5.9, -3.9, "Will vs a\nclimbing guard", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -7.2, -4.1, "zone weak, at\nthe bubble", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[0], "Over: the weak guard is free")
# Under: inside zone right, at the bubble over the RG
p = Play(off, under_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "C", (0.2, 0.75)); go_to(p, "RG", (0.25, 1.0))
go_to(p, "RT", (0.3, 4.0)); go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.7)); go_to(p, "LG", (0.3, -2.3)); go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.6))
go_to(p, "RB", (-0.9, 2.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, 0.7)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.2, -0.6), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-8.2, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 7.0), title=False)
ring(f, p, "RG", color=GREEN, r=1.05)
dashed(f, p, [(0.6, 1.4), (2.4, 1.8), (3.65, 1.9)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
say(f, p, 5.9, 4.4, "Mike vs a\nclimbing guard", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -7.2, 4.1, "zone strong, at\nthe bubble", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1], "Under: the strong guard is free")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Over and Under are the same eleven players making opposite bets.** The Over puts its linemen where the
offense has the most blockers and asks a linebacker to cover the weak side's bubble. The Under puts two
men on the line on the tight end's side to win the edge, sends its best interior rusher to the side
where he is hardest to double, and asks the Mike to handle the strong side's bubble. Neither is better.
A defense that can play both, and switch between them without substituting anyone, gives the offense a
different blocking problem from the same personnel, which is exactly why most 4-3 teams carry both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**The dialects.** Not every staff means the same thing by "Under." For some, it is enough that the line
leans away from the tight end: Monte Kiffin's Tampa 2 defenses, and Lovie Smith's Bears after them, set the
under tackle on the weak side and the nose on the strong A gap but usually kept the Sam off the ball, and
some coaches call that an Under; others call it an Over from the linebackers' point of view, or give it a
name of their own. Others reserve "Under" for the version in @fig-over-under, with the Sam on the line.
Some teams set their ends by side (left and right) rather than by strength, so the ends never move and only
the tackles and linebackers shift. And the strong end in an Over may play a 5, a 6 or a 7. When a coach
draws "his" Over or Under on a whiteboard, read the alignments, not the word.
:::

## When the strength moves

The relative call has a cost, and offenses collect it. If the front is set by the tight end, moving the
tight end moves the front.

```{python}
#| label: fig-strength-shift
#| fig-cap: "A tight-end shift against the 4-3 Over. Left, before: the tight end (Y) lines up on the right, so the Over leans right. He shifts across the formation, behind the tackles, to the left (dashed), and must be set for a full second before the snap. Right, after: the strength is now the left, and the Over has to lean left. The 3-technique and the 1-technique trade sides (dotted outlines are where they started), the Sam and the Will trade sides, and the Mike slides over a gap, all in the second or two between the shift and the snap. Here the ends stay on their sides; their techniques don't change, but which one is the strong end does."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-8.4, 8.6), window=(-3.6, 6.6), title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(-1.2, 4.8), (-2.1, 3.0), (-2.1, -3.0), (-1.2, -4.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4)
say(f, p, -2.85, 0.0, "the tight end shifts left", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.9)
say(f, p, 5.9, -5.5, "strength:\nright", color=style.INK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
title(axes[0], "Before the shift: Over to the right")
p = Play(line("short") + [te(-1)], over_front(-1), los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-8.6, 8.4), window=(-3.6, 6.6), title=False)
old = {"DT": (1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), "NT": (1.0, T("1", -1), "1"), "SAM": (4.2, 6.2, "S"), "WILL": (4.5, -2.0, "W"),
       "MIKE": (4.5, 0.8, "M")}
for k, (d0, w0, lab) in old.items():
    ghost(f, p, d0, w0, lab)
dashed(f, p, [(1.0, T("3", 1) - 0.7), (2.25, 0.6), (1.6, T("3", -1) + 0.75)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
dashed(f, p, [(1.0, T("1", -1) + 0.6), (1.0, T("1", 1) - 0.65)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
dashed(f, p, [(4.2, 5.3), (5.6, 0.0), (4.4, -5.3)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.1)
dashed(f, p, [(4.5, -1.2), (4.5, 1.25)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.1)
say(f, p, 5.9, 5.6, "strength:\nleft", color=style.INK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -2.6, 0.0, "3 and 1 trade places; S and W swap", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.9)
title(axes[1], "After: the Over has to lean left")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

@fig-strength-shift is why tight-end shifts and motions became so common
([Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) has the offense's side).
One player jogs a few yards; five defenders have to re-set, and they have about a second and a half to do
it. Several things can go wrong. A tackle who is still moving at the snap is a tackle who hasn't got his
stance, and a one-gap lineman without a stance has lost his head start. Two linebackers who don't hear the
new call fill the same gap. And the offense learns something either way: if the 3-technique crosses the
center every time the tight end moves, the offense now knows his rule and can put him wherever it wants
him, for instance on the side away from the play it is about to run.

Defenses have answers, and each one is a trade. Some don't flip the line at all on a late shift and just
re-set the linebackers, accepting a front that leans the "wrong" way for one snap. Some set the line by
the field or by the running back instead, so a tight-end shift doesn't move anything. Some teach a
check-word that kills the movement. Every one of those answers gives up some of the precision the front was
built on, which is the point of shifting in the first place.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you pick "4-3 Over" from a menu and the line appears, already leaning the right way, every time.
On a real field the front is a *rule*, not a picture. The call says "Over" and the defenders work out
where that means for this formation, then work it out again when the tight end moves, often while the
offense is still shifting. A defense whose front is a step late re-setting is a defense the offense has
already beaten before the ball is snapped.
:::

## The wide-9: stretch the front to rush the passer

The Over and the Under move the line sideways. The wide-9 front stretches it. You met the
[wide-9](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-9) end in
[05-01](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd): a defensive end set well outside the tight end (or where
one would be), in a sprinter's stance, built to run around the tackle. Put one on each side of a four-man
line and the whole front changes shape.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wide-nine-front
#| fig-cap: "A wide-9 front against a shotgun offense with a tight end on the right (receivers outside the picture). Orange shading: each rusher's path to the quarterback. The two ends start far outside and arc around the tackles; the tackles (a 1 and a 3) attack their gaps. Blue shading: the price. Between each end and the nearest tackle is a running lane several yards wide (the off-tackle lanes, numbers are their width at the line), and on a run the linebackers have to fill them (dashed orange): the Sam on the right, the Will on the left. The wider the ends, the better the rush angle and the longer the linebackers' trip."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -(4.8 + 2.3), "w9"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "1"),
       D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("wide9", 1), "w9"),
       D("WILL", "LB", 5.0, -2.9, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 5.0, 0.6, "M"), D("SAM", "LB", 4.8, 4.6, "S")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 5.0))
f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.0, 11.0), window=(-8.4, 8.2), title=False)


def corridor(f, p, pts, width=1.0, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.15):
    """A shaded band of `width` yards along the polyline pts (absolute (d, w))."""
    pts = np.array(pts, float)
    left, right = [], []
    for i in range(len(pts)):
        a, b = pts[max(i - 1, 0)], pts[min(i + 1, len(pts) - 1)]
        v = b - a
        n = np.array([-v[1], v[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(v) * width / 2
        left.append(pts[i] + n); right.append(pts[i] - n)
    poly = np.vstack([left, right[::-1]])
    xs, ys = _P(f, p, poly[:, 0], poly[:, 1])
    f.ax.add_patch(Polygon(np.column_stack([xs, ys]), closed=True, fc=color, ec="none", alpha=alpha, zorder=0.9))
    xs, ys = _P(f, p, pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
    f.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=1.4, zorder=1.0)
    f.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                                   color=color, lw=1.4, zorder=1.0))


corridor(f, p, [(0.2, -7.1), (-1.6, -6.9), (-4.4, -3.9), (-5.6, -1.4)], width=1.2)
corridor(f, p, [(0.2, 7.1), (-1.6, 6.9), (-4.4, 3.9), (-5.6, 1.4)], width=1.2)
corridor(f, p, [(0.2, -0.7), (-1.5, -0.8), (-4.0, -0.4)], width=1.0)
corridor(f, p, [(0.2, 2.35), (-1.5, 2.3), (-4.0, 0.7)], width=1.0)
lane(f, p, T("3") + 0.55, 7.1 - 0.55, 0.15, 2.5, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.12)
lane(f, p, -7.1 + 0.55, T("1", -1) - 0.55, 0.15, 2.5, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.12)
say(f, p, 1.35, (T("3") + 7.1) / 2, f"{7.1 - T('3') - 1.1:.1f} yd", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 1.35, (-7.1 + T("1", -1)) / 2, f"{abs(T('1', -1) + 7.1) - 1.1:.1f} yd", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
dashed(f, p, [(4.3, 4.4), (2.6, 4.6)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
dashed(f, p, [(4.5, -3.1), (2.6, -3.6)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
say(f, p, -2.4, -9.5, "the end's\narc", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -2.4, 9.5, "the end's\narc", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 6.7, 6.0, "Sam fills the\nlane on a run", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 6.7, -6.0, "Will fills the\nlane on a run", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**Why play it?** Pass rush, first and last. An end in a wide-9 has the longest runway and the best angle
to the quarterback of any defensive lineman. The tackle in front of him has to kick-slide a long way to meet
him, and the tight end, if there is one, can't reach him without help. Rushing from there, a fast end gets
to the quarterback's depth in fewer steps than he would from a 5, and he gets there on an angle that turns
the tackle's shoulders. The front also simplifies the linemen's lives: as 05-01's Jim Washburn put it, they
attack, and think about gaps only as the place they are attacking.

**What does it cost?** Look at the blue shading in @fig-wide-nine-front. With the ends that far out, the
space between each end and the nearest tackle, the *off-tackle* lane, is three to five yards wide at the
line, and on a run the ends are going upfield, not closing it. Somebody else has to: on the tight end's
side the Sam, on the other side the Will, often with a safety coming down behind them. The wide-9 moves
run defense from the defensive line to the linebackers. A wide-9 team with linebackers who are late, or a
3-technique who gets moved off the ball and widens the lane from the inside, gives up the long runs that
gave the front its reputation.

So which is it, a pass-rush front that can't stop the run, or something else? The Philadelphia Eagles
have played it in two very different seasons, and the numbers tell the story better than the reputation.
The table is computed from nflverse play-by-play when this book is built.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (Eagles run defense in two wide-9 seasons, from nflverse play-by-play)"
from IPython.display import Markdown
from gridiron.data import pbp


def run_defense(season, team="PHI"):
    """Designed runs only (no scrambles), regular season: team's yards per game and per carry, with ranks."""
    df = pbp(season, columns=["season_type", "play_type", "defteam", "rushing_yards", "qb_scramble", "game_id"])
    runs = df[(df.season_type == "REG") & (df.play_type == "run") & (df.qb_scramble == 0)]
    games = runs.groupby("defteam")["game_id"].nunique()
    g = runs.groupby("defteam")["rushing_yards"].agg(["sum", "mean"])
    g["ypg"] = g["sum"] / games
    rk_ypg = g["ypg"].rank(method="min").astype(int)
    rk_ypc = g["mean"].rank(method="min").astype(int)
    return {"Season": season, "Front coach": "", "Rush yd/game": f"{g.loc[team, 'ypg']:.0f}",
            "Rank (of 32)": int(rk_ypg[team]), "Yd/carry": f"{g.loc[team, 'mean']:.2f}",
            "Rank (of 32) ": int(rk_ypc[team]), "League yd/carry": f"{runs['rushing_yards'].mean():.2f}"}


rows = [run_defense(2011), run_defense(2017)]
rows[0]["Front coach"] = "Washburn (DL coach)"
rows[1]["Front coach"] = "Schwartz (coordinator)"
tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows)
cols = list(tbl.columns)
md = ["| " + " | ".join(c.strip() for c in cols) + " |", "|" + "|".join([":--", ":--"] + ["--:"] * (len(cols) - 2)) + "|"]
md += ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in rw) + " |" for rw in tbl.itertuples(index=False)]
Markdown("\n".join(md))
```

The 2011 Eagles, in Jim Washburn's first season, tied for the league lead in sacks and were a below-average
run defense on a per-carry basis. The 2017 Eagles, under Jim Schwartz, the coordinator who had run the
wide, attacking front with Washburn in Tennessee, allowed the fewest rushing yards per game in the league
and won the Super Bowl.[^widedata] Same alignment, opposite results against the run. What changed was mostly
what stood inside and behind the ends: Fletcher Cox, drafted in 2012, at the 3-technique, and linebackers and
safeties who arrived in the lanes on time. "It always looked like you should be able to run the ball against
it," the analyst Charles Davis said of Schwartz's front, "but when you have people like Fletcher Cox inside
and some of those other guys, it's not as easy to run the ball against it as you think."[^davis]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The wide-9 can't stop the run." It gives the run a bigger target, and it makes the players behind the
ends more important. With an interior that holds its ground and linebackers who fill fast, it can be the
best run defense in the league, as the 2017 Eagles were. Judge a wide-9 front by its linebackers.
:::

## The 46 and the bear front

The even fronts so far lean, or stretch, a four-man line. The last one in this chapter crushes it
together, and for a few seasons in the 1980s it was the most feared defense in football.

### Buddy Ryan's defense

**Buddy Ryan** was a defensive line coach who had won a Super Bowl with the 1968 Jets and coached
Minnesota's line after that before the Chicago Bears made him their defensive coordinator in 1978. A
Korean War veteran from a farm in Oklahoma, he was blunt, combative, loyal to his players and openly
contemptuous of offenses, including his own team's. His problem in Chicago was the problem every defense of
that era had: offenses ran the ball out of two-back formations, the I-formation and the split backs, with
a fullback leading the way and guards pulling, and they ran it well. His answer, worked out over several
seasons and in full bloom by 1981, was to put more players near the ball than the offense could
block.[^ryan]

He named it after a player. Doug Plank was a hard-hitting safety whom Ryan moved down from his deep spot
to play, in effect, as a linebacker. "He circled my number three times," Plank recalled, "and said, 'we're
going to call this the 46 defense.'"[^plank] So the [**46 defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-46-defense)
is not a count of anything: it is Plank's jersey number. Plank retired after the 1982 season, three years
before the defense became famous.

```{python}
#| label: fig-46-plate
#| fig-cap: "The 46 against a two-back I-formation (21 personnel). On the line: the weak end a yard or two outside the left tackle, a 3-technique on each guard and a nose head-up on the center, so the center and both guards are covered (green rings): that is the bear front. Both outside linebackers are on the tight end's side, one on his inside shoulder (W) and one outside him (S). The Mike stands over the right tackle, the strong safety (ringed: the original 46) over the left tackle, at linebacker depth. Eight men within five yards of the ball; behind them, two cornerbacks pressed on the receivers and one free safety deep."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
BEAR = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, -(3.2 + 1.5), "5w"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
        D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("WILL", "LB", 1.3, 4.1, "W"), D("SAM", "LB", 1.4, 6.0, "S"),
        D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 3.2, "M"), D("SS", "S", 4.5, -3.2, "SS")]
SECONDARY = [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.0, "CB"), D("FS", "S", 11.0, -1.6, "FS")]
p = Play(off, BEAR + SECONDARY, los=35, to_go=10)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8.6, 13.6), title=False)
for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
    ring(f, p, k, color=GREEN, r=1.0, lw=1.6)
ring(f, p, "SS", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, r=1.25)
say(f, p, -2.9, 0.0, "center and both guards covered: the bear", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 6.3, -3.4, "SS: the '46'", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 3.3, 7.6, "both outside\nlinebackers\non the TE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 3.8, -15.0, "press, man", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 3.8, 15.0, "press, man", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.4, -6.4, "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-46-plate from the middle out. The heart of it is the line: a nose head-up on the center and a
3-technique on each guard. That interior, three men covering the center and both guards, is called a
[**bear front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bear-front), after the team that made it famous. Outside
it, the weak end lines up a yard or two outside the weak tackle. Then Ryan did something no 4-3 did: he
moved *both* outside linebackers to the tight end's side, one on the tight end's inside shoulder to jam
his release and one outside him. The Mike stands over the strong tackle, and the strong safety comes down
to linebacker depth over the weak tackle.[^46wiki] Count them: eight defenders within five yards of the
ball, against seven blockers. Behind them, the two cornerbacks press the wide receivers in man coverage and
a single safety plays deep. And on many snaps five, six or seven of those eight came after the quarterback.

(Strictly, a nose head-up on the center makes the bear an *odd*-looking front. It lives in this chapter
because it was built by a 4-3 team, out of 4-3 personnel, and because it is the logical end of the even
front's idea: decide which offensive linemen to leave free, and leave none.)

### Why covering the guards breaks the blocking

Every run scheme in [Part 3](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) needs at least one interior
lineman who isn't covered. Zone needs him to start a double team and climb. Power, counter and the trap need
him to pull. The iso needs the guards to drive two defensive linemen apart while a fullback hits the
linebacker. The bear front takes all of that away at once.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bear-iso
#| fig-cap: "The bear front against an I-formation iso (a lead play: the fullback leads through the hole onto a linebacker), simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates. 1: before the snap the center and both guards are covered (green rings): nobody inside is free. 2: at the snap every offensive lineman has a defender in front of him, so every block is one-on-one; there is no double team to move the nose and no guard free to climb. 3: the fullback, the only blocker left, takes the Mike; the strong safety (orange ring), whom nobody can reach, is already filling. 4: the safety meets the back in the hole, about a yard past the line (X). Against a front that leaves a guard uncovered, that guard would have climbed to the second linebacker."
def bear_iso():
    off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    p = Play(off, BEAR, los=35, to_go=None)
    # every lineman blocks the man on him (a little give and take, no climbing)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.15, -0.35), speed=1.0); go_to(p, "NT", (0.75, -0.25), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.2, 2.15), speed=1.0); go_to(p, "ST", (0.7, 2.6), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.15, -2.1), speed=1.0); go_to(p, "WT", (0.75, -2.45), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.0, -4.3), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "WE", (-0.2, -5.0), "path", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 3.75), speed=1.4); go_to(p, "WILL", (0.9, 4.1), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.6, 5.6), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "SAM", (1.1, 6.1), "path", speed=0.5)
    # the fullback leads through the right A gap and up to the Mike, who comes to meet him
    go_to(p, "FB", (2.9, 2.2), "path", speed=5.0, via=[(-1.0, 0.9)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.2, 2.5), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.25)
    # the strong safety: unblocked, he reads and fills the hole
    go_to(p, "SS", (1.3, 0.8), "path", speed=4.6, delay=0.35, via=[(3.0, -0.6)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.0, -1.2), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (0.7, 0.85), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-3.4, 0.6)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (0.85, 0.85), "run", speed=0.6)
    return p


def bear_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    if t < 0.05:
        for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
            d, w = play.position(k, t)
            x, y = _P(fld, play, d, w)
            fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.0, fc="none", ec=GREEN, lw=1.5, zorder=7))
    if t >= 1.4:
        spot(fld, play, 1.0, 0.85, ms=9)


P_BEAR = bear_iso()
animation_or_strip([(P_BEAR, 0.0, ""), (P_BEAR, 0.45, ""), (P_BEAR, 0.95, ""), (P_BEAR, 1.55, "")],
                   notes=["center and both guards\ncovered: nobody is free",
                          "every block one-on-one:\nno double team, no climber",
                          "the fullback takes the Mike;\nnobody can reach the SS",
                          "the safety fills the hole\nand makes the tackle"],
                   rings=(("SS", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-7.8, 8.6), window=(-8.4, 6.4), after=bear_marks,
                   width_in=5.2)
```

Work through what the bear does to each kind of play.

- **No double teams.** With the center and both guards covered, nobody inside can help a neighbor without
  leaving his own man free. Every interior block is one-on-one, against three linemen chosen precisely
  because they win one-on-one. The double team that moves a defensive tackle off the ball, the foundation of
  inside zone and power alike, never forms.
- **No climbers.** The linebackers behind a four-man front survive by beating a guard who climbs to them. In
  the bear, the guards can't climb: a guard who leaves his 3-technique has let a penetrator into the
  backfield. So the linebackers, and the safety playing linebacker, run to the ball with no one in their way.
  An offense with a fullback can send him at one of them. There are two, plus a seventh and eighth man on the
  tight end's side.
- **No pullers.** Pull a guard on power or a trap, and the 3-technique he was covering has a free run into
  the backfield before the play has started. The plays that beat aggressive one-gap fronts by letting
  defenders through and then hitting them from the side need a lineman who can leave; the bear leaves none.
- **No easy pass protection.** On a pass, the three interior rushers each have a blocker of their own, the
  center can't slide to help, and the outside linebackers stacked on the tight end's side create more
  rushers on that side than the offense has blockers. Ryan's defense then decided, every snap, which of the
  eight to send.

### The 1985 Bears

The result was one of the great defensive seasons in NFL history. The 1985 Bears went 15–1 and allowed
198 points, the fewest in the league; they also led the league in yards allowed and takeaways. In the
playoffs they shut out the Giants 21–0 and the Rams 24–0, and then beat the New England Patriots 46–10 in
Super Bowl XX on January 26, 1986.[^bears85] New England ran the ball 11 times in that game for 7 yards, still
the Super Bowl record for fewest rushing yards, and the Bears sacked New England's quarterbacks seven times,
tied for the most in any Super Bowl; the defensive end Richard Dent was the game's MVP.[^sb20] After the game, Ryan's players carried him off the
field on their shoulders, alongside the head coach, Mike Ditka, with whom he had feuded all season.

### Why it disappeared

The 46's one loss in 1985 told the rest of the league how to beat it. On December 2, on Monday Night
Football, the Miami Dolphins beat the Bears 38–24. Miami's quarterback, Dan Marino, had one of the
quickest releases in the game, and the Dolphins' receivers won the one-on-one matchups the 46's man
coverage gave them (the same source as the alignments above). An eight-man front with three defensive backs behind it is built for a two-back,
two-receiver offense. Against three receivers and a quarterback who throws before the rush arrives, its
strength becomes its problem.

```{python}
#| label: fig-46-quick
#| fig-cap: "Why the 46 faded: the same eight-man front against three receivers and a quick throw (simulated, BDB-format tracking; the left side of the field). 1: the offense spreads out: a slot receiver (H) inside the split end (X). The 46 has three defensive backs, so the slot receiver is covered by the strong safety, a box player, from inside the box (ringed). 2: at the snap the defense sends six (orange), and the quarterback takes a three-step drop. 3: H runs a quick slant; the safety, starting six yards inside and four yards deep, is a step late. 4: the ball is out in about 1.4 seconds, before any rusher arrives, and H has room in front of him with only the deep safety to beat."
def quick_vs_46():
    off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0, "R"),
                          O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H")]
    dfn = [q for q in BEAR] + [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.0, "CB"), D("FS", "S", 11.5, -2.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
    p.route("X", r.slant(2.0, 7.0))
    p.route("H", r.slant(1.0, 7.0))
    p.man("LCB", "X")
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.5, -5.2), "path", speed=4.2, delay=0.3, via=[(4.6, -4.6)])
    for k in ("WE", "WT", "NT", "ST", "WILL", "SAM"):
        p.rush(k, speed=3.4)
    for k, end in [("LT", (-1.6, -4.4)), ("LG", (-1.3, -2.4)), ("C", (-1.3, -0.3)), ("RG", (-1.3, 2.2)),
                   ("RT", (-1.5, 4.0)), ("Y", (-1.8, 5.4)), ("RB", (-4.6, 1.2))]:
        go_to(p, k, end, speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.0, 0.8), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.4)
    go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -4.5), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.6)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    p.pass_to("H", t=1.35)
    return p


P_QUICK = quick_vs_46()
animation_or_strip([(P_QUICK, 0.0, ""), (P_QUICK, 0.6, ""), (P_QUICK, 1.3, ""), (P_QUICK, 2.0, "")],
                   notes=["three receivers: a box safety\nmust cover the slot (H)",
                          "six rush; three-step drop",
                          "the slant breaks inside;\nthe safety is a step late",
                          "ball out before the rush\narrives: room to run"],
                   rings=(("SS", style.DEFENSE), ("H", style.THIRD)), lateral=(-17.5, 4.5), window=(-7.4, 13.6),
                   width_in=5.4)
```

Offenses spent the next decade doing to the 46 what @fig-46-quick shows. Three-receiver sets pulled a
linebacker or the safety out of the box or left a slow man covering a fast one. Quick, timed throws got the
ball out before the extra rushers arrived. And as the run-and-shoot and the West Coast offense spread
through the league ([The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) tells that story),
the two-back offense the 46 was designed to strangle became the exception. The full 46 is now a
curiosity, but its pieces never left. Ryan coached it again in Philadelphia, as head coach from 1986 to
1990, and in Houston and Arizona; his sons Rex and Rob carried versions of it into the 2000s.

The bear front itself is the part that survives. Near the goal line, against two tight ends or a
fullback, defenses still cover the center and both guards to take away the interior double teams. And the
idea behind it, decide which interior linemen to leave uncovered, is alive in the
[tite front](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) that NFL defenses use against inside runs today: the tite
covers the center and the tackles' inside shoulders, the bear covers the center and the guards, and both
are answers to the same question.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The 46 means four linemen and six linebackers." The digits in 4-3 and 3-4 count players, so this is a
natural guess, and it's wrong. The 46 is named for Doug Plank's jersey number. Counted the usual way, it
has four men with their hands down, three linebackers and a safety playing a fourth, and three defensive
backs behind them.
:::

## From two backs to three receivers: the even front in nickel

The fronts in this chapter grew up against offenses with two backs and one tight end, **21 personnel**.
That offense has nearly disappeared: in 2025, 21 personnel was about 7% of NFL snaps, while 11 personnel,
one back, one tight end and three wide receivers, was about 59%.[^personnel] The four-man even front didn't
disappear with it. What changed was everything behind the line.

```{python}
#| label: fig-under-vs-11
#| fig-cap: "The same Under line against two offenses. Left, 21 personnel (I-formation): the base 4-3, with the Sam on the line outside the tight end and the strong safety down in the box as an eighth man (shaded: the box). Right, 11 personnel (a slot receiver H on the left in place of the fullback): the four linemen do not move, because the tight end, and so the strength, has not moved. The Sam leaves the field for a nickel back ($), who lines up between the left tackle and the slot receiver; the weak end widens because there is no tight end on his side; and the strong safety rotates down to do the Sam's old job on the tight end. The box goes from eight to seven."
def box(f, p, w0, w1, d1=5.9):
    lane(f, p, w0, w1, -0.2, d1, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.07, ls=(0, (2, 2)))


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.7))
off21 = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
dfn = under_front(+1) + [D("SS", "S", 5.3, -4.4, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 11.5, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off21, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-11.2, 9.0), window=(-8.4, 12.8), title=False)
box(f, p, -5.6, 7.0)
say(f, p, 7.4, -7.5, "8 in the box", color=style.INK, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 6.5, 6.2, "Sam on\nthe line", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
title(axes[0], "Under vs 21 personnel (base 4-3)")
off11 = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.5, "H")]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-6.4) if q.key == "WE" else q for q in under_front(+1, sam=False)]
dfn += [D("NB", "NB", 4.6, -7.4, "$"), D("SS", "S", 5.6, 6.6, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 12.0, -0.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off11, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-11.2, 9.0), window=(-8.4, 12.8), title=False)
box(f, p, -5.6, 7.9)
say(f, p, 7.6, -1.4, "7 in the box", color=style.INK, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 7.9, -8.6, "nickel\nfor the Sam", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 8.2, 6.6, "SS does the\nSam's job", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -3.1, -7.6, "end widens:\nno TE here", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1], "Same line vs 11 personnel (nickel)")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

@fig-under-vs-11 shows the pattern most even-front teams follow.

**The line is set by the run strength, and it stays.** The tight end hasn't moved, so the front's rule
hasn't changed: the Under still leans away from him, the 3-technique still on the weak guard. The four
linemen are the same players in the same spots. That's the great practical virtue of a four-man even front.
It is the same from base to nickel, so the defensive line doesn't need a second set of rules.

**The third linebacker is the part that changes.** Against a third wide receiver, the Sam has three
choices, and two of them are bad. He can stay in the box, where he can't cover the slot receiver. He can
walk out over the slot, an [apex](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-apex) alignment between the box and the
receiver, where a linebacker is now covering a receiver in space. Or he can leave the field for a nickel
back, a cornerback who can cover and is big enough to tackle. Most NFL defenses choose the third, and the
[nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel) package that results, four linemen, two linebackers and
five defensive backs, is the **4-2-5** you will meet as a front family of its own in
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd).

**Someone still has to do the Sam's old job.** On the right of @fig-under-vs-11 the strong safety rotates
down over the tight end to take the D gap, which turns the coverage behind him into a one-deep shell. That
is roughly how Pete Carroll's Seattle defenses of the 2010s played it, with a big strong safety, Kam
Chancellor, as a de facto linebacker. The other option is to keep two safeties deep and let the box be
six against six blockers, the "light box" that [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
measured, and accept that the offense can run. That choice, and its arithmetic, is the subject of
[Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

**The ends get wider when the tight end leaves.** With no tight end on his side, there is no D gap there;
the weak end's job is the C gap and the edge, and on a likely passing down nothing stops him from
setting up in a wide-9's stance and angle. Watch an even front against 11 personnel on third down and you
will often see one end in a 5 on the tight end's side and the other as wide as a wide-9 on the open side.

The trend is running the other way again. In 2025 NFL offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on
41.7% of plays, the highest share since Next Gen Stats began tracking in 2016, and defenses answered by
playing base personnel on 29.7% of snaps, up from a low of 20.5% in 2023.[^personnel2] The 4-3 Over and
Under, with a real Sam on the field, are coming back with the tight ends and fullbacks.

## Reading the front from the broadcast

The diagrams in this book look down from above. The broadcast doesn't. The main camera sits high on one
sideline, near the line of scrimmage, so you see the line from the side, and the one thing a front is
made of, which shoulder each lineman is on, runs straight away from you into the screen.

```{python}
#| label: fig-broadcast
#| fig-cap: "The same 4-3 Under from two cameras. Top, the broadcast's high sideline camera (the offense going left to right, the tight end on the near side). Shoulders line up one behind another, so you can't measure techniques; instead, find two landmarks: the tight end (the end of the line, here nearest the camera), and the gap in the defensive line, the guard with nobody across from him (green). In an Under the empty guard is on the tight end's side; in an Over it is on the other side. Bottom, the end-zone replay camera, looking down the line from behind the offense: now every shoulder is visible and you can read the techniques directly (the 3 on the left guard, the 1 on the center's right shoulder)."
def project(pts, cam, target, focal=1.0):
    """Pinhole camera: world points (downfield d, offense's LEFT, height) -> screen (x, y) and depth."""
    C, Tg = np.asarray(cam, float), np.asarray(target, float)
    fwd = (Tg - C) / np.linalg.norm(Tg - C)
    right = np.cross(fwd, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]); right /= np.linalg.norm(right)
    up = np.cross(right, fwd)
    P = np.atleast_2d(np.asarray(pts, float)) - C
    z = P @ fwd
    return focal * (P @ right) / z, focal * (P @ up) / z, z


def camera_view(ax, players, cam, target, labels, notes=(), green=(), xlim=None, ylim=None):
    """Draw a 3-D-projected field window and upright players. `players`: (key, side, d, w, label)."""
    W = lambda d, w, h=0.0: (d, -w, h)   # noqa: E731  offense's right is -left
    for d in range(-10, 21, 5):           # yard lines
        xs, ys, _ = project([W(d, w) for w in np.linspace(-26.6, 26.6, 40)], cam, target)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8 if d % 10 == 0 else 0.5, zorder=1)
    xs, ys, _ = project([W(0, w) for w in np.linspace(-26.6, 26.6, 40)], cam, target)
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.2, alpha=0.7, zorder=1.5)       # line of scrimmage
    for w in (-26.6, 26.6):               # sidelines
        xs, ys, _ = project([W(d, w) for d in np.linspace(-10, 20, 30)], cam, target)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    order = sorted(players, key=lambda q: -project([W(q[2], q[3])], cam, target)[2][0])
    for key, side, d, w, lab in order:   # far players first
        (x0,), (y0,), (z0,) = project([W(d, w, 0.0)], cam, target)
        (x1,), (y1,), _ = project([W(d, w, 1.85)], cam, target)
        s = 60.0 / z0
        col = style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
        ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=col, lw=4.2 * s, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=3 + 1 / z0)
        mk = "o" if side == "off" else "s"
        fc = style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE_TINT
        ax.plot([x1], [y1], marker=mk, ms=6.5 * s, mfc=fc, mec=col, mew=1.0, zorder=3.1 + 1 / z0)
        if key in green:
            ax.plot([x0], [y0], marker="o", ms=17 * s, mfc="none", mec=GREEN, mew=1.6, zorder=3 + 1 / z0)
        if key in labels:
            dx, dy, txt = labels[key]
            ax.annotate(txt, (x1, y1), xytext=(x1 + dx, y1 + dy), fontsize=6.9, ha="center", va="center",
                        color=GREEN if key in green else (style.OFFENSE_DARK if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE_DARK),
                        fontweight="bold", zorder=12,
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.6, color=style.MUTED, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=3),
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))
    for x, y, txt in notes:
        ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    if xlim: ax.set_xlim(*xlim)
    if ylim: ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
    ax.set_facecolor(style.TURF)


SCENE = ([(q.key, "off", q.d, q.w, q.label) for q in line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"),
                                                                      O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]]
         + [(q.key, "def", q.d, q.w, q.label) for q in under_front(+1)]
         + [("SS", "def", 8.0, 5.5, "SS"), ("FS", "def", 12.0, -3.0, "FS")])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 6.6), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.0, 1.05]})
side_cam, side_tgt = (1.5, -42.0, 21.0), (2.0, 0.0, 0.0)
camera_view(axes[0], SCENE, side_cam, side_tgt,
            labels={"Y": (-0.02, -0.075, "tight end:\nstrong side"), "RG": (-0.11, -0.03, "empty guard"),
                    "DT": (0.10, 0.05, "the 3, far side"), "SAM": (0.10, -0.06, "Sam on the line")},
            green=("RG",), xlim=(-0.36, 0.42), ylim=(-0.25, 0.16))
axes[0].set_title("Broadcast: high sideline camera", fontsize=8.8, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
end_cam, end_tgt = (-21.0, 0.0, 10.0), (3.0, 0.0, 0.0)
camera_view(axes[1], SCENE, end_cam, end_tgt,
            labels={"DT": (-0.08, 0.06, "3: on the LG's\noutside shoulder"), "NT": (0.0, 0.10, "1: center's\nright shoulder"),
                    "RG": (0.06, -0.075, "uncovered"), "SAM": (0.07, 0.07, "Sam, outside Y")},
            green=("RG",), xlim=(-0.44, 0.44), ylim=(-0.30, 0.17))
axes[1].set_title("End-zone replay: behind the offense", fontsize=8.8, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

From the high sideline shot, you can't measure a technique. What you can find, every snap, are two
landmarks.

1. **The tight end.** He is the strength, so find him first: the man at the end of the line, a step
   off the tackle, often with a hand on his knee. If he is on the near side of the screen, the strong side
   is near; if he is on the far side, it is far.
2. **The empty guard.** You can't see shoulders from the sideline, but you can see *holes*. Look along the
   defensive line for the gap: the guard with nobody across from him. **If the empty guard is on the tight
   end's side, it's an Under; if it's on the other side, it's an Over.** The 3-technique is on the other
   guard, and you can say "3-tech away from the tight end" (Under) or "toward" (Over).

Then add the details. A linebacker standing on the line outside the tight end is the Under's Sam. Ends
lined up so wide they are nearly out of the shot are a wide-9. Three linemen packed across the middle with
no empty guard at all, and extra men stacked on the tight end's side, is a bear. And when the replay
comes, from the end-zone camera, check your read: from behind the offense, every shoulder is visible.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chicago Bears, Super Bowl XX (1985 season)"}
**The game:** Bears 46, Patriots 10, January 26, 1986, at the Louisiana Superdome. New England gained 7
yards on 11 rushes and 123 yards in all, and had negative total yardage at halftime.[^sb20b]

**What to notice:**

- Before each early-down snap, count the defenders within five yards of the ball. Eight is the 46.
- The interior: a nose on the center and a tackle on each guard. Watch the guards at the snap. Do they ever
  get to a linebacker?
- The outside linebackers. Both on the tight end's side, one jamming him at the line. Notice how rarely the
  tight end gets cleanly into a route.
- When New England spreads out, watch the safeties and linebackers who have to cover. That is where the
  46 was always vulnerable, even in its greatest game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks, 2013 season"}
**The season:** Pete Carroll's fourth year in Seattle, and the best version of his 4-3 Under: a 323-pound
former defensive tackle, Red Bryant, as the strong-side 5-technique end, the Sam on the line outside the
tight end, a quick 3-technique on the weak side and a pure pass-rushing weak-side end (Carroll's name for
him is the *Leo*).[^bryant] Seattle led the NFL in scoring defense from 2012 through 2015, the first team of
the Super Bowl era to do it four years running, and in Super Bowl XLVIII it beat the Denver Broncos, who had
just set the league record for points in a season, 43–8.[^seattle4] Carroll traces the scheme to 1977, when he
was a graduate assistant at Arkansas under the defensive coordinator Monte Kiffin: "It was a one-gap principle
defense way back then," he said. "He taught me everything I know about defense."[^carrollkiffin]

**What to notice:** find the tight end, then look for the Sam standing on the line outside him and the big
end in the 5 beside him. On runs to that side, watch the two of them meet the blockers at the line and
turn the ball back inside, Gus Bradley's "turn everything back inside to our big guys." Then look across
to the weak side for the 3-technique, alone against a guard.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles, Super Bowl LII (2017 season)"}
**The game:** Eagles 41, Patriots 33, February 4, 2018, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis. Jim Schwartz's
wide-9 front had been the NFL's best run defense that season, and in the fourth quarter its signature play
was a pass rush: with about two minutes left and Philadelphia ahead by five, the end Brandon Graham, lined up
inside over a guard on that snap, beat his man and stripped the ball from Tom Brady, and the Eagles recovered.[^sb52]
<!-- VERIFY: Graham aligned inside (at defensive tackle) on the Super Bowl LII strip-sack. -->
